newsitem.title: MALI: Malian opposition demonstrates on eve of poll.
newsitem.headline: Malian opposition demonstrates on eve of poll.

text.p: Well over one thousand Malian opposition supporters took to the streets of the capital Bamako on Saturday on the eve of elections they are boycotting, witnesses said.
The marchers, from 20 opposition parties, called on people not to vote in the presidential election, seen as a key test of democracy in the impoverished West African state.
"No to elections," the marchers shouted, also demanding the departure of President Alpha Oumar Konare, who now faces only one challenger in the poll -- businessman Hamadou Maribatrou Diaby.
The constitutional court on Thursday ruled that an opposition appeal for the elections to be postponed was inadmissable.
The opposition had called for the poll to be delayed after severe organisational problems marred an April 13 parliamentary election. The court has scrapped those results.
It had argued that a one-week delay announced by Konare could create confusion. The court did not accept this argument.
Mali, praised for its 1992 democratic transition, has run into trouble with this year's elections -- the second multi-party elections since independence from France in 1960.
Malians turned out in force on April 13 only to find that problems with voter cards, lists or ballot materials prevented them from voting.

Konare's Alliance for Democracy in Mali party ended its election campaign in a packed stadium in Bamako on Friday, where thousands of supporters gathered to be told by party dignitaries that they should go out and vote.
The government has closed schools and colleges after students threw stones and burned Konare campaign posters on Monday.

Representatives of 15 non-political interest groups, among them the main Islamic body, unions and the business association, condemned both government and opposition politicians for failing to reach an agreement on holding the election.

Political analysts in Bamako compare a wave of student demonstrations, power and water strikes with the tension which gripped the city before the 1991 overthrow of former one-party ruler General Moussa Traore by the military.
Konare, a historian elected in 1992, has steered the country on a course of economic liberalisation. He has won praise from the World Bank and the United States for his efforts.
